sources.text:
Far-right figure Milo Yiannopoulos deported from US
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported to the United Kingdom after his arrest by US immigration authorities.
The US Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country on Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the US legally in May 2019.
A immigration judge had issued a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.
Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
"He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws," a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.
Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment. He has not posted on his X social media account since Thursday.
Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticising feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
"Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts," Yiannopoulos wrote on X last year.
The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening.
Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News.
He resigned from the company in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologised for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.
Yiannopoulos' arrest on Thursday comes amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump's immigration crackdown.
Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos' arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities.
"I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene," Loomer wrote on X.
Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his "Troll Academy Tour" across college campuses nationwide.
Fights broke out when some students protested Yiannopoulos' appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time, Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos' cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.
In recent years, Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism.
Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following anti-Semitic comments that the rapper has since apologised for.

sources.text:
Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right commentator who was one of President Trump’s most prominent early supporters and later worked as an adviser for Ye (formerly Kanye West), was deported to his native Britain on Friday, per a statement by the Department of Homeland Security obtained by the New York Times.
Yiannopoulos had been arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on Thursday. The DHS later shared a mug shot of Yiannopoulos on social media, responding to a TMZ report on the commentator’s arrest. The post said that Yiannopoulos had “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws” after entering the country legally in 2019 and that a final order for removal was issued by an immigration judge on July 22.
One of the most recognizable fixtures of conservative media during Trump’s rise to the presidency and the early years of his first term, Yiannopoulos gained his profile through inflammatory commentary targeting Muslims, immigrants, transgender individuals, feminists and other groups, oftentimes courting the spotlight through controversial college campus appearances.
In 2017, Yiannopoulos resigned from Breitbart after video resurfaced in which he appeared to condone sexual relationships between adults and minors. The controversy also prompted the Conservative Political Action Conference to rescind his speaking invitation and Simon & Schuster to cancel publication of his planned book.
Yiannopoulos has also supported Trump’s aggressive immigration-enforcement policies. In 2025, he called for ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, as well as immediate deportation for anyone unable to prove they were legally in the country.
In the years since his Breitbart tenure, Yiannopoulos has continued working outside the spotlight. He briefly interned for former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene and became an adviser to Ye, working on the rapper’s barely-launched 2024 presidential bid. A source familiar with Ye’s operation told TheWrap in May that Yiannopoulos continued to advise the rapper. During the same period, Yiannopoulos posted a series of antisemitic messages around Ye’s public apology for his past antisemitic statements, including posts published immediately before and after the apology.

US deports right-wing provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos
Washington (United States) (AFP) – Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported to his home country of Britain, the US government said Saturday.
Issued on:
Yiannopoulos, an early supporter of Donald Trump who has voiced support for the president's immigration crackdown, has largely fallen out with the Trump movement.
He was arrested Thursday at New Orleans International Airport and deported the following day by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement to AFP.
After arriving in the United States in 2019 and overstaying his visa, he was issued a final order of removal in July "after failing to show up for his immigration hearing," the department said.
The 41-year-old entered the public eye a decade ago, casting himself as a gay crusader for free speech and an enemy of "political correctness," but was widely accused of being racist and misogynistic.
He wrote for the right-wing US news outlet Breitbart News and backed Trump during the 2016 election campaign but has more recently been critical of the US leader.
Right-wing influencer Laura Loomer hailed his arrest, boasting on X that she was "the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump."
ICE is tasked with carrying out Donald Trump's anti-immigration crackdown, and many Americans consider its methods brutal. Federal agents shot dead two American citizens in January as they protested anti-immigrant enforcement raids in Minneapolis.
In September 2025, Yiannopoulos posted on X: "Total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty."

The series is filming in Atlanta and is expected to premiere in 2027. Its young Mystery Inc. lineup features Maxwell Jenkins as Fred, Tanner Hagen as Shaggy, Abby Ryder Fortson as Velma and Mckenna Grace as Daphne.
Netflix’s modern reimagining follows old friends Shaggy and Daphne during their final summer at camp, where they become caught up in a haunting mystery involving a lonely Great Dane puppy that may have witnessed a supernatural murder.

The Trump administration deported far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos to the United Kingdom shortly after his arrest in New Orleans one day earlier.

Far-right blogger Laura Loomer, an influential outside adviser to the Trump administration who had sparred with Yiannopoulos in the past, told The Washington Post she was “100 percent” the reason the activist had been detained.

sources.news_title: British far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the U.S., DHS says
sources.text: British right-wing provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos was deported Friday to the United Kingdom, according to a spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security. Yiannopoulos was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement Thursday at a Louisiana airport after overstaying his visa, DHS said. The conservative figure was being held by ICE in Louisiana, where several ICE facilities have served as the final stop for thousands of migrants in U.S. President Donald Trump’s deportation push. Here’s what you need to know about Yiannopoulos’ deportation, arrest and his controversial path through the far-right orbit and conservative politics. Who is Milo Yiannopoulos? Born in England to British and Greek parents, Yiannopoulos came to the US, where he built a career as a conservative firebrand who leaned into controversy through his writing for the far-right website Breitbart News, speeches and online presence. He was an outspoken supporter of Donald Trump during his presidential campaign in 2016 and gained fans who appreciated his complete abandonment of political correctness. Many of his views drew outrage from many who argued the racist and hateful language was an attempt to stoke tensions on campus and should not be platformed by colleges and universities. He has equated feminism with cancer, said America “has a Muslim problem,” disparaged transgender people and started a scholarship exclusively for young, White men. He has embraced the outcry that often erupts from his comments, reportedly proclaiming himself the “most fabulous supervillain on the internet.” While he previously said he was gay – and featured his sexuality as a significant part of his gadfly brand – he has recently said he no longer identifies as such. Why was he detained? Yiannopoulos entered the U.S. legally on May 14, 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the DHS said in a statement announcing his arrest on X. A judge issued a final order of removal for Yiannopoulos on July 22, after he failed to appear at an immigration hearing, the agency said. Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana. He was deported “back to his home country” Friday, DHS told CNN. After his arrest, far-right influencer and Trump ally Laura Loomer – who has bitterly feuded with Yiannopoulos – wrote in a post on X Friday that she had reported him to ICE and the FBI. There’s no indication that any report from Loomer had a connection to his arrest, which came at a time when ICE arrests have been happening more frequently at U.S. airports. It is unclear how Yiannopoulos had been operating in the U.S. prior to 2019, as he had been employed and appeared regularly at public speaking events across the country since at least 2015. In 2017, he said he was in the U.S. on an O-1 visa for immigrants of “extraordinary ability.” CNN has reached out to DHS for further details. CNN is working to determine if Yiannopoulos has legal representation. What is he known for? Yiannopoulos became more well-known while the conservative landscape was undergoing a tidal change, as then-presidential candidate Trump was rallying a furiously antiestablishment base, and alt-right ideas were inching closer to the mainstream. Until 2017, he honed his voice as an outspoken senior editor at Breitbart News, where he wrote columns and gave speeches titled things like “10 Things Milo Hates About Islam” and “Sorry, Girls! But The Smartest People In The World Are All Men.” He made it his mission to take on what he viewed as traditionally left-leaning college establishments that year, embarking on a “Dangerous F*ggot” bus tour of U.S. universities and college campuses – in the name of promoting free speech and undermined voices – during which he argued rape culture on campuses didn’t exist, compared social justice to a disease and at times mocked individual students. He was typically invited to speak by conservative student organizations. Yiannopoulos’ acerbic and at times hateful speech attracted the fury of students who argued his views should not be platformed. Several of his campus events were met with protests, including one at the University of California, Berkeley that was canceled after demonstrations became violent. He positioned himself as one of Trump’s passionate supporters, sometimes jokingly referring to the president as “Daddy.” The conservative at times connected the wave of support he had received with the same conservative movement that paved Trump’s path to the presidency. “People are tired of being told how to live, how to speak, what language they can use,” Yiannopoulos told CNN in 2017. “The strength of feeling in my crowds, the enthusiasm for me from the audiences is the same – the same instinct, the same sort of motivating force (that) put Trump in the White House.” When asked for comment about Yiannopoulos’ arrest, the White House referred CNN to DHS. How did his platform dwindle? Yiannopoulos came under intense scrutiny in February 2017 after he made comments appearing to condone pedophilia. Yiannopoulos resigned from Breitbart amid the backlash and offered a rare apology but said the media distorted his comments. In the span of a day, he lost his book deal with publishing giant Simon & Schuster and he was disinvited from speaking at the powerful Conservative Political Action Conference. Following the backlash, Yiannopoulos focused largely on renouncing his sexual orientation as a gay man. His Telegram account, which hasn’t seen new posts in more than a year, said he was opening a clinic in Florida that would help “men plagued by same-sex attraction.” He also told Tucker Carlson last year, “mainstreaming homosexuality in the Republican Party is the great regret of my life.” Twitter banned Yiannopoulos in 2016. His Facebook account was also taken down in 2019, further limiting his online presence. In a 2022 Telegram post, he said he was an unpaid intern to former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, a lightning-rod Republican from Georgia. Yiannopoulos also continued to have his eye on national politics, working on the 2024 presidential campaign of Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, who fell from grace after praising Adolf Hitler and making a series of antisemitic comments. Ye performed at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans Friday, the same day Yiannopoulos was deported. After Elon Musk bought Twitter, now known as X, Yiannopoulos had his account reinstated and remained prolific online. Yiannopoulos posted on X as recently as Thursday, the day federal officials detained him in Louisiana. What has he said about immigration? Yiannopoulos has frequently called for aggressive immigration enforcement in posts on his X account over the last year. After Trump returned to the White House on a campaign to dramatically increase deportations of undocumented people, Yiannopoulos insisted the administration needed to make good on that promise. “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” Yiannopoulos said in a June 2025 X post. “It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.” In September 2025, nearly two weeks after a Mexican man was fatally shot by ICE in Minneapolis, Yiannopoulos called for “total legal immunity for ICE agents when they’re on duty.” He had also called for ICE checkpoints in heavily trafficked areas in California, like gas stations and intersections, and “on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the U.S. legally.” By Elizabeth Wolfe, Eduardo Cuevas, Sydney Bishop, CNN

Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right commentator and former Breitbart News editor with ties to President Donald Trump and rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, was deported by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Friday after being taken into custody earlier this week, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek in an email Saturday.
The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom" and was sent "back to his home country."
He was arrested by ICE at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) in Kenner, Louisiana, according to the spokesperson, who noted that "Yiannopoulos legally entered the country on May 14, 2019, through New York City, New York."
"He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws," the spokesperson continued.
For years, Yiannopoulos was a vocal supporter of stricter immigration enforcement, often criticizing illegal immigration and backing mass deportation policies championed by Trump and other immigration hardliners.
A final order of removal was issued July 22 by an immigration judge after Yiannopoulos failed to show up for an immigration hearing, according to the DHS spokesperson.
Newsweek has reached out to Yiannopoulos by email Saturday.
"DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this," the spokesperson said. "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."
Yiannopoulos said in 2017, after resigning as an editor from Breitbart News, that he owned an O-1 visa, which works as a temporary work permit for people with “extraordinary ability or achievement in fields like science, business, education, athletics, or the arts.”
His removal also comes as the Trump administration continues a sweeping immigration crackdown that has dramatically increased arrests and deportations since Trump returned to office in January 2025.
According to data from Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and ICE, roughly 590,600 deportations have been recorded between Trump's return to office and July 11, 2026.
The administration has framed the effort as part of what Trump has called the largest deportation campaign in U.S. history, while critics argue it has swept up significant numbers of immigrants with no criminal records.
Yiannopoulos' Past Support for Deportation
Yiannopoulos has previously been vocal in his support of ICE and deportations, writing in an X post in June 2025 that California "needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally."
Yiannopoulos wrote on X last year: “Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts.”
In an interview with podcaster Joe Rogan in 2016, he said he supported deportation but clarified, "I mean bad immigrants," adding, "I don't mean handsome, charming, successful, blonde-haired British immigrants….It's about culture."
His own deportation has drawn attention since it mirrors the type of immigration enforcement he previously advocated. DHS said he was ordered removed after overstaying his visa and failing to attend an immigration hearing.
The department encouraged undocumented immigrants to leave voluntarily through the CBP Home app, which it said offers financial assistance and transportation for those who choose to self-deport.
Meanwhile, conservative political activist Laura Loomer claimed credit for Yiannopoulos' ICE detention, resharing a post from March in which she'd accused him of living in the U.S. with an expired visa. "Milo Yiannopoulos is in ICE custody after I exposed his illegal alien lifestyle," the Trump ally wrote on X.
Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, also said on X Friday, "Milo Yiannopoulos deserves full due process, and like everyone else, should not be subject to abusive conditions in detention. But he appears to be reaping what he has sowed, so I can't find myself sympathetic."
Where Is Milo Yiannopoulos From?
Yiannopoulos was born in Kent, England, and is a British citizen. Before becoming a prominent figure in U.S. conservative politics, he built a career in the United Kingdom as a technology journalist and commentator. He later moved to the United States, where he gained national attention through his work at Breitbart News and his support for Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.
His profile grew rapidly during the rise of the alt-right movement, with speaking tours, media appearances and a large social media following helping make him one of the era's most recognizable conservative commentators. While his influence declined after a series of controversies, he remained active in right-wing political circles and later resurfaced through his work with Ye, running a short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for the rapper.
Yiannopoulos stepped away from the campaign in December 2022 after the rapper made antisemitic comments that Ye has since apologized for.
Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jenni Fink and Anthony Murray.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom

sources.news_title: British far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US, DHS says
sources.text:
British right-wing provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos was deported Friday to the United Kingdom, according to a spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security.
Yiannopoulos was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement Thursday at a Louisiana airport after overstaying his visa, DHS said.
The conservative figure was being held by ICE in Louisiana, where several ICE facilities have served as the final stop for thousands of migrants in President Donald Trump’s deportation push.
Here’s what you need to know about Yiannopoulos’ deportation, arrest and his controversial path through the far-right orbit and conservative politics.
Who is Milo Yiannopoulos?
Born in England to British and Greek parents, Yiannopoulos came to the US, where he built a career as a conservative firebrand who leaned into controversy through his writing for the far-right website Breitbart News, speeches and online presence.
He was an outspoken supporter of Donald Trump during his presidential campaign in 2016 and gained fans who appreciated his complete abandonment of political correctness.
Many of his views drew outrage from many who argued the racist and hateful language was an attempt to stoke tensions on campus and should not be platformed by colleges and universities. He has equated feminism with cancer, said America “has a Muslim problem,” disparaged transgender people and started a scholarship exclusively for young, White men. He has embraced the outcry that often erupts from his comments, reportedly proclaiming himself the “most fabulous supervillain on the internet.”
While he previously said he was gay – and featured his sexuality as a significant part of his gadfly brand – he has recently said he no longer identifies as such.
Why was he detained?
Yiannopoulos entered the US legally on May 14, 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the DHS said in a statement announcing his arrest on X.
A judge issued a final order of removal for Yiannopoulos on July 22, after he failed to appear at an immigration hearing, the agency said.
Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana.
He was deported “back to his home country” Friday, DHS told CNN.
After his arrest, far-right influencer and Trump ally Laura Loomer – who has bitterly feuded with Yiannopoulos – wrote in a post on X Friday that she had reported him to ICE and the FBI.
There’s no indication that any report from Loomer had a connection to his arrest, which came at a time when ICE arrests have been happening more frequently at US airports.
It is unclear how Yiannopoulos had been operating in the US prior to 2019, as he had been employed and appeared regularly at public speaking events across the country since at least 2015. In 2017, he said he was in the US on an O-1 visa for immigrants of “extraordinary ability.” CNN has reached out to DHS for further details.
CNN is working to determine if Yiannopoulos has legal representation.
What is he known for?
Yiannopoulos became more well-known while the conservative landscape was undergoing a tidal change, as then-presidential candidate Trump was rallying a furiously antiestablishment base, and alt-right ideas were inching closer to the mainstream.
Until 2017, he honed his voice as an outspoken senior editor at Breitbart News, where he wrote columns and gave speeches titled things like “10 Things Milo Hates About Islam” and “Sorry, Girls! But The Smartest People In The World Are All Men.”
He made it his mission to take on what he viewed as traditionally left-leaning college establishments that year, embarking on a “Dangerous F*ggot” bus tour of US universities and college campuses – in the name of promoting free speech and undermined voices – during which he argued rape culture on campuses didn’t exist, compared social justice to a disease and at times mocked individual students.
He was typically invited to speak by conservative student organizations.
Yiannopoulos’ acerbic and at times hateful speech attracted the fury of students who argued his views should not be platformed. Several of his campus events were met with protests, including one at the University of California, Berkeley that was canceled after demonstrations became violent.
He positioned himself as one of Trump’s passionate supporters, sometimes jokingly referring to the president as “Daddy.” The conservative at times connected the wave of support he had received with the same conservative movement that paved Trump’s path to the presidency.
“People are tired of being told how to live, how to speak, what language they can use,” Yiannopoulos told CNN in 2017. “The strength of feeling in my crowds, the enthusiasm for me from the audiences is the same – the same instinct, the same sort of motivating force (that) put Trump in the White House.”
When asked for comment about Yiannopoulos’ arrest, the White House referred CNN to DHS.
How did his platform dwindle?
Yiannopoulos came under intense scrutiny in February 2017 after he made comments appearing to condone pedophilia.
Yiannopoulos resigned from Breitbart amid the backlash and offered a rare apology but said the media distorted his comments. In the span of a day, he lost his book deal with publishing giant Simon & Schuster and he was disinvited from speaking at the powerful Conservative Political Action Conference.
Following the backlash, Yiannopoulos focused largely on renouncing his sexual orientation as a gay man. His Telegram account, which hasn’t seen new posts in more than a year, said he was opening a clinic in Florida that would help “men plagued by same-sex attraction.” He also told Tucker Carlson last year, “mainstreaming homosexuality in the Republican Party is the great regret of my life.”
Twitter banned Yiannopoulos in 2016. His Facebook account was also taken down in 2019, further limiting his online presence.
In a 2022 Telegram post, he said he was an unpaid intern to former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, a lightning-rod Republican from Georgia.
Yiannopoulos also continued to have his eye on national politics, working on the 2024 presidential campaign of Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, who fell from grace after praising Adolf Hitler and making a series of antisemitic comments.
Ye performed at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans Friday, the same day Yiannopoulos was deported.
After Elon Musk bought Twitter, now known as X, Yiannopoulos had his account reinstated and remained prolific online. Yiannopoulos posted on X as recently as Thursday, the day federal officials detained him in Louisiana.
What has he said about immigration?
Yiannopoulos has frequently called for aggressive immigration enforcement in posts on his X account over the last year.
After Trump returned to the White House on a campaign to dramatically increase deportations of undocumented people, Yiannopoulos insisted the administration needed to make good on that promise.
“There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” Yiannopoulos said in a June 2025 X post. “It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”
In September 2025, nearly two weeks after a Mexican man was fatally shot by ICE in Minneapolis, Yiannopoulos called for “total legal immunity for ICE agents when they’re on duty.”
He had also called for ICE checkpoints in heavily trafficked areas in California, like gas stations and intersections, and “on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

A CNN anchor dug up tweets by far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement after he was detained by the very agency.
On Friday, CNN anchor Brianna Keilar looked back at posts by Yiannopoulos that supported aggressive ICE enforcement as she spoke about his arrest at a New Orleans airport.
"Just a year ago, Yiannopoulos appeared to be quite supportive of ICE's approach," Keilar noted as she read posts by him. One 2025 tweet read, "California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections, and government buildings with on-the-spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they're in the U.S. legally."
Keilar asked veteran political commentator Bill Kristol what he thought and what he's seen from the Trump administration in terms of how they're messaging Yiannopoulos' arrest.
"I don't know if they're going to message about it or they're just showing, 'See, we want to deport anyone who's here illegally,'" Kristol said. "I mean, they are fanatics about mass deportation. We shouldn't, we really can't lose sight of the forest for the trees."
Kristol said that Yiannopoulos is "getting a little bit of maybe his own medicine here since he was gloating about the deportation of others, especially people with dark-color skins or foreign accents and so forth."
Yiannopoulos is a British national, according to the Department of Homeland Security, so "he's going to be put on a plane back to London," Kristol pointed out. "He's not going back to the Central African Republic like some people from Central America are being deported in the middle of the night there," Kristol said.
"He's not like these 300,000 Haitians who came here, got Temporary Protected Status, contributed to their communities, had low crime rates, were living lawful lives here in the U.S.," Kristol added. "The administration removes their Temporary Protected Status, and presto, they're illegal."

The Department of Homeland Security on Friday confirmed the arrest of Milo Yiannopoulos, the former conservative media icon who previously worked for Breitbart News and went on to work for Kanye West.
DHS confirmed that Yiannopoulos entered the U.S. legally in 2019 via New York City. He overstayed his visa, however, and received a final order of removal from an immigration judge on July 22. He did not attend his immigration hearing.
"Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now," DHS posted on X. "We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return."
Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election as a conservative firebrand. He emphasized his homosexuality and flamboyant image as he maintained ostensibly far-right political positions.
His career fell off after the election, when a previously unreleased tape of him discussing homosexual relationships with underage boys went public.
He later became an intern for now former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., before acting as Kanye West's chief of staff for years.
Ben Whedon is the Chief Political Correspondent for Just the News. Follow him on X.

Deported! Milo Yiannopoulos Was Just Sent Packing by ICE
On Joe Rogan in 2016 he carved out one exception: “handsome, charming, successful, blonde-haired British immigrants.” He didn’t make the cut.
Milo Yiannopoulos, the far-right provocateur who once called for ICE checkpoints to carry out “on the spot” deportations of anyone in the country illegally, was himself deported on August 28. It’s a near-perfect closing of the loop: the loudest cheerleader for aggressive immigration enforcement removed by the very agency he championed.
DHS told USA TODAY that ICE sent Yiannopoulos, “an illegal alien from the United Kingdom, back to his home country.” Agents arrested him a day earlier at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana. He had entered the US legally through New York on May 14, 2019, and, in the department’s words, “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.” An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to show up for his hearing.
The political backdrop is messier than the paperwork. Laura Loomer, a former ally turned enemy, had been publicly calling him an illegal overstayer since late 2024 and says she reported him to ICE, DHS, and the FBI. After the arrest she claimed credit on X, posting “Loomered.” The Telegraph, citing senior US sources, reported that his visa status “was brought to attention after he fell out of favour with senior officials over his increasingly hostile remarks” — including a recent appearance on Candace Owens’s show, where he called Trump “bought, paid for, owned and operated” by Israel.
The department leaned into the irony, posting his mugshot and using the arrest to promote its self-deportation offer of $3,000 and a free flight home.
The fall is a long way from where he started. Yiannopoulos built his name as a right-wing commentator before the first Trump administration, writing for Breitbart News and touring college campuses where he attacked feminism, Islam, Black Lives Matter, and transgender people.

sources.news_title: Far-right British provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported after immigration arrest in US
sources.text:
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported back to the United Kingdom after his arrest by American immigration authorities, U.S. officials said Saturday.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country on Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the U.S. legally in May 2019. A immigration judge had issued a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.
Yiannopoulos was arrested Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
"He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws," a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.
Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment. He has not posted on his X social media account since Thursday.
Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
"Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts," Yiannopoulos wrote on X last year.
The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening.
Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned from the company in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.
Yiannopoulos' arrest on Thursday comes amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump's immigration crackdown.
Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos' arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities.
"I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene," Loomer wrote on X.
Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his "Troll Academy Tour" across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested Yiannopoulos' appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time, Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos' cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.
In recent years, Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022, he was an intern for former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to the Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye.
Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologized for.

sources.text:
The former Breitbart editor, once an outspoken Trump supporter, faces removal as MAGA rival Laura Loomer claims credit
British conservative commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by US immigration authorities in Louisiana and faces deportation after allegedly overstaying his legal status and failing to appear for an immigration hearing.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested the 41-year-old former Breitbart editor at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana, on August 27, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
"Yiannopoulos legally entered the country on May 14, 2019, through New York City," DHS said, describing him as an "illegal alien" who "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws."
An immigration judge issued Yiannopoulos a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to appear for his hearing, the department said. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal.
The arrest quickly spilled into a bitter feud within the MAGA movement. Conservative activist and Trump ally Laura Loomer celebrated Yiannopoulos' detention and claimed she had personally alerted authorities to his immigration status. The Daily Caller reported that scrutiny of his status intensified after he began criticizing President Donald Trump's immigration policies.
The episode also carries an ironic twist, as Yiannopoulos has himself repeatedly backed tough immigration enforcement, including sweeping restrictions and mass deportations.
Once one of Trump's most flamboyant online supporters, Yiannopoulos famously referred to him as "Daddy" during the 2016 campaign. Their relationship later deteriorated sharply, with the British commentator accusing Trump of betraying supporters.
Yiannopoulos subsequently joined Kanye 'Ye' West as the rapper mounted an abortive 2024 presidential bid, serving as his campaign manager. He also helped arrange Ye's controversial 2022 dinner with Trump at Mar-a-Lago. Earlier that year, he had worked as an unpaid intern for then-Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene.
Yiannopoulos has remained a favorite target of progressive activists and much of the mainstream media, which has frequently labeled him "far-right." He has rejected such descriptions, arguing that they are used to marginalize outspoken conservative figures and turn political controversy into character assassination.
His confrontational style has repeatedly generated outrage, however. Among other issues, he drew attention years ago to Britain's grooming-gang scandals, accusing authorities and the media of ignoring the abuse of vulnerable girls because officials feared accusations of racism or Islamophobia.
Yiannopoulos' career suffered a major setback in 2017 after old remarks about sexual relationships involving minors resurfaced, costing him a publishing deal and forcing his resignation from Breitbart.
The White House has not publicly intervened in his immigration case.
